chapter: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
title: Jam session gatekeepers: Big Bill Moore, Lockjaw Davis and Monk's lateness
summary: Players had to audition to sit in; Monk used to leave while someone filled in.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: The only thing that will save it, man, is if ______ joins, becomes legalized again, that people have a place to go jam and sing. It's organized, most jams is organized. I remember the one in California, that guy, that Big Bill Moore. You had to see Big Bill Moore before you could sit in. He wasn't the biggest tenor player, but he'd say if you couldn't play enough to make sense with the guys up there, he wouldn't let you sit in.
And Lockjaw Davis did the same thing in business. You ever heard that?
You had to go in the back room to audition for him.
The Charlie Christian days, all those days.

Yeah. Everybody thought Monk was late but Monk. This is what Eddie told me. He says, Monk has a job, it's his job, when he come to work and somebody would be playing piano, so he'd go out two or three hours and come back. He said that when Monk was coming to the Five Spot, to him it was the same as me and ______, expect somebody to be there playing in his place.
